rationale:
Quota: 1 long video, 3 Shorts, 0 carousels. Everything stays inside the GLP-1 focus.

**Long video:** the queue can't use its first two items. Foundayo What to Expect was made on 11-24 and must never be scripted again. Mounjaro vs Ozempic has been live since 11-23. The next item is Serious Risks: How Rare?, which is held, so this is a re-time and fix of the existing script, not a new one. It is also the analytics playbook's next priority. The radar's peaking NAION story (Health Canada's 25 Nov warning on top of the FDA class label change) gives it a timely, label-based hook. The body rests on the US labels and the FDA safety notice, so it can be checked in depth. Five of the last seven long videos were search-demand formats, so a Lane A video is fine today.

**Shorts:** all three are felt or practical moments. None is a study, news or label-change topic, and none repeats a recent Short.
- **08:00 (S1):** a fresh hair angle on our best proven Short topic: why shedding seems to start months in.
- **13:00 (S2):** a gallbladder spin-off of L1. The last gallbladder Short was 10-26, outside the 30-day window.
- **20:00 (S3):** Thanksgiving Day felt moment, linked to the Thanksgiving video. Loose stools the morning after hasn't been used as a holiday angle yet.

The two GI Shorts cover different organs and symptoms. L1 covers several body systems, so no single system gets three pieces. I skipped the mammogram story (a news topic and a small conference study) and nothing on the radar was marked reject.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) vs dulaglutide (Trulicity) in the SURPASS-CVOT randomized heart-outcomes trial (NEJM 2025): adults with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, about 13,300 people, median follow-up about 4 years. Covers the main heart and stroke result, death from any cause, A1C and weight, stomach side effects and stopping rates, what a non-inferiority trial with an active comparator can and can't tell you, and questions to ask your prescriber or cardiologist.
pieces.angle: Keep the planned structure, with these changes. Working title: 'Mounjaro vs Trulicity for Heart Disease: What the SURPASS-CVOT Trial Found'. Thumbnail stays 'FEWER HEART EVENTS?' with subtext 'tirzepatide vs dulaglutide · type 2 diabetes'. Opening: 'about thirteen thousand adults with type 2 diabetes and heart or blood-vessel disease', the exact per-arm primary rates, HR 0.92 and CI from the NEJM paper, then 'not worse than dulaglutide; it did not prove it was better.' Second payoff: death from any cause per arm, said to be a secondary outcome that can't confirm a benefit on its own. Say per-arm A1C (-1.66 vs -0.88 points) and weight (-11.6% vs -4.8%), and say GI adverse events were more frequent on tirzepatide. Name Lilly as the funder. Quote each label's Section 1 exactly and mention a CV indication only where the live label prints it. Close with prescriber questions and 'don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.'
pieces.working_title: Mounjaro vs Trulicity: Which Protected the Heart More?
pieces.why: An approved-drug head-to-head against tirzepatide (our best long format), with real brand-name search demand, built on one settled NEJM randomized trial that is easy to fact-check first time. It doesn't overlap with the dropped Serious Risks video, today's hair, gallbladder and diarrhea Shorts, or any live video. | fact-check: The trial is real and the topic fits the channel, with good evidence behind it. SURPASS-CVOT was published in NEJM on 17 Dec 2025 (PubMed 41903177). It was a double-blind, active-comparator, non-inferiority trial in adults with type 2 diabetes and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, median follow-up about 4 years. The primary outcome was cardiovascular death, heart attack or stroke. Rates were about 12% on tirzepatide and 13% on dulaglutide, HR 0.92: non-inferior (p=0.003) but not superior (p=0.09). Death from any cause was lower on tirzepatide, a secondary outcome. A1C fell 1.66 vs 0.88 points and weight fell 11.6% vs 4.8%. Tirzepatide had more GI adverse events, and overall adverse events were similar. Fixes needed before scripting: (1) Population size. 6,586 + 6,579 = 13,165 were randomized, so 'about 13,300' is wrong. Use 'about thirteen thousand' or the paper's exact randomized count. (2) The title 'Which Protected the Heart More?' suggests one drug won. The trial did not show superiority, so use a neutral question that doesn't hint at a winner. (3) Death from any cause must be framed as a secondary outcome that does not prove benefit. Use the paper's exact hedge and CI, and don't call it 'lower risk of dying' without that hedge. Never put it in the title or thumbnail. (4) Take the exact per-arm rates, HR and 95% CI from the NEJM paper, not from news coverage. (5) Name Eli Lilly (maker of both drugs) as the funder. (6) Section 1 of each label: Trulicity's US label carries a cardiovascular risk-reduction indication (from REWIND). Check whether the live Mounjaro PI (27 Aug 2026) has added a CV indication, quote only what it prints, and never imply an indication from this trial. (7) The trial arm labels (tirzepatide up to 15 mg vs dulaglutide 1.5 mg) are the dose limit; no other dose talk. (8) The 'Don't switch' safety line is good. Keep the no-switching framing all through: the video compares trial results, not which medicine to choose. (9) Confirm no existing SURPASS-CVOT or Trulicity long video is on the channel.

pieces.why:
Rising search ahead of January. The title sits next to big Ozempic videos for suggested traffic, and the body rests on settled primary sources (a physiology review, label section 12.3, FDA 21 CFR 101.81), so it should pass the fact-check first time. | fact-check: The topic is sound. It's an evidence-led myth-buster that fits the natural-GLP-1 pillar, keeps the medicine and food clearly apart, and has low misinformation risk. Most of the brief's claims check out, but there are three things to fix before scripting and two to watch.

Verified while screening:
(a) Shukla et al., Diabetes Care 2015, 'Food Order Has a Significant Impact on Postprandial Glucose and Insulin Levels', is a pilot study in adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes, all on metformin. It measured glucose and insulin at 0, 30, 60 and 120 min. It did NOT measure GLP-1, so chapter 4 must make no GLP-1 claim from this paper. The 16-adult paper that measured GLP-1 is a separate publication. Use it only with its own citation after a content-check fetch, or leave it out. Still to do: confirm n=11 against the full text.
(b) The 2025 joint advisory exists: Mozaffarian D et al., 'Nutritional Priorities to Support GLP-1 Therapy for Obesity: A Joint Advisory From the ACLM, ASN, OMA and TOS', Am J Lifestyle Med 2025 (also in AJCN and Obesity). Its exact sentence is: 'Smaller, more frequent meals and avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment can help alleviate symptoms.' It sits in the GI side-effect / nausea section. Quote the whole sentence at that scope. Don't cut it down to only the fibre clause, and don't turn it into 'avoid fibre on GLP-1'.

Must fix:
1) Chapter 3 wording. The FDA claim under 21 CFR 101.81 is a heart-disease risk claim: soluble fibre from whole oats, as part of a diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol, 'may reduce the risk of heart disease'. Calling it a 'claim about lowering cholesterol' makes it sound stronger than it is. Quote the model claim from the eCFR text, with the 3 g a day soluble fibre condition, and mention cholesterol only as how the claim is explained.
2) Thumbnail. Muted and on its own, 'OATS = OZEMPIC?' spreads the myth. Add labelled subtext that answers it: 'A SMALL NUDGE VS A MEDICINE'. Or use 'OATS VS OZEMPIC?'.
3) Guardian intro line. It's unverified. Fetch the article and credit it by name and date. If it can't be found, cut the line rather than describing the trend vaguely.

Carry forward:
- Half-life figures exactly as the labels print them (semaglutide PI 12.3, about 1 week; tirzepatide PI 12.3, about 5 days) and in the Holst review's own wording (under about 2 minutes).
- Chapter 2: no figures unless they come from a fetched paper, labelled with its population and size.
- The SURMOUNT-1 average with its full population and 'placebo plus counseling'.
- Never imply that fibre, oats or eating order replace or match the medicine.
- No 'oatzempic' recipe and no other 'nature's Ozempic' products (berberine, supplements).
- The kidney caveat on protein.
- The constipation line in label wording.

pieces.topic: Semaglutide (Ozempic) and chronic kidney disease in type 2 diabetes: what the randomized FLOW kidney-outcomes trial (NEJM 2024) found, what the US Ozempic label's kidney indication covers, what CKD and eGFR/urine albumin mean, the heart and survival secondary results, side effects and stopping rates, and questions to ask your doctor about kidney checks
pieces.angle:
Evergreen explainer built on settled evidence, 9–11 min. Sources:
- FLOW, Perkovic et al., NEJM 2024 (PubMed): 3,533 adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease, semaglutide vs placebo, median follow-up about 3.4 years, stopped early at a planned interim analysis for efficacy
- Ozempic US PI Section 1 and 6.1 (FDALabel effective 1 Jun 2026, version 20, Ozempic only; never borrow another label's date)
- NIDDK or NHS CKD pages for definitions, each with its own URL and live date

Opening:
- Sentence 1 names semaglutide (Ozempic), asks the title's question and answers it with a 'you' moment. Example: 'If you have type 2 diabetes and kidney disease: in a big randomized trial, fewer people on semaglutide had serious kidney events than on placebo.'
- Payoff at 15–30 s: the primary composite per arm as in the paper (about 18.7% vs 23.2%, HR 0.76), with the population on the card.
- Never say 'Short answer.', no list opening, no 'meet the trial' scene.

Chapters, named as searched questions:
1. What is CKD, and what are eGFR and urine albumin? Definitions from NIDDK or NHS.
2. What did FLOW find? The primary result and what the composite includes, exactly as the paper words it.
3. Heart and survival: secondary outcomes as printed with both arms. Say they're secondary.
4. What the US label says: quote Section 1's kidney indication word for word with its population. It's for adults with type 2 diabetes and CKD, not CKD without diabetes, and not shown for tirzepatide.
5. Side effects: serious adverse events 49.6% vs 53.8% as a whole-trial result. GI effects in label wording, and stopping because of adverse events per arm as printed. Always 'adverse events', never 'side effects', for trial figures.
6. Questions to ask your doctor: how often to check eGFR and urine albumin, and other medicines. Include the dehydration line in label wording, the low-blood-sugar caveat with insulin or a sulfonylurea, and the Medication Guide's emergency pancreatitis line verbatim, followed by the fixed don't-stop line.

Rules:
- No dose numbers, switching or stopping advice, and no 'now' or 'new'.
- 'Linked to' and 'may' wording kept exactly as the source has it. One result per sentence with its population.
- Lists of 3 items at most. Re-hook every 45–75 s. Land the last new fact before 80%. Never end a chapter on a warning card.
- One subscribe ask after the chapter 2 payoff.
- Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' Post note watch-next target: Side Effects.
- Thumbnail: 'KIDNEYS TOO?' with one calm labelled character, no organ imagery.
pieces.working_title: Semaglutide (Ozempic) and Kidney Disease: Does It Help?
pieces.why: Replacement L4. It rests on one landmark randomized trial plus a label with a known, verified date (Ozempic, FDALabel 1 Jun 2026). It has never had a long video, uses a searched brand next to big Ozempic videos, and covers a new body system for today.

pieces.topic: An itchy rash or itchy patch of skin away from the injection spot on tirzepatide: what the US label says about hypersensitivity reactions vs placebo, and which signs mean emergency care
pieces.angle:
Keep the 08:00 'Is this normal?' set-up, the tight arm (90–120 words, exact count logged), the mix at masking 0.02 or lower, no skin close-ups, no subscribe or link line, and the Exp G post note: the target is the Side Effects long video.
Sentence 1, with matching on-screen text: 'Itchy rash on tirzepatide? The label says most allergic-type reactions in trials were skin reactions.' Spoken, 'most' stands in for the label's 'the majority', which is the label's own claim, not one we're adding. Do not say 'most weren't serious'.
By 6 s, show one stat copied from Zepbound PI section 6.1, using the non-immediate figure only. Spoken: 'about three and a half in a hundred on tirzepatide versus about three in a hundred on placebo had reactions that started after the first day.' Card: '3.5% VS 2.7% PLACEBO · NON-IMMEDIATE HYPERSENSITIVITY REACTIONS · ZEPBOUND LABEL, STUDIES 1 AND 2: ADULTS WITH OBESITY, OR OVERWEIGHT PLUS A WEIGHT-RELATED CONDITION (STUDY 2: TYPE 2 DIABETES ONLY), UP TO 72 WEEKS'. Optional second line, if the word count allows: 'Severe reactions: 0.1% vs none on placebo (section 5.6).' Never add the two types together or write '5 vs 3'.
Cite only the Zepbound label (DailyMed updated 16 Nov 2026; PI 'Revised: 11/2026') and the separate Zepbound Medication Guide URL with its own 'Revised: 11/2026' date. Never use Mounjaro's date. Don't say what causes it, and keep it separate from injection-site reactions.
Replace the untagged line with: 'A new rash or itching is a reason to contact your prescriber promptly.'
Next, the emergency card: the Medication Guide's allergy list copied word for word after checking it against the guide PDF, followed by its 'stop using … and get medical help right away' wording. 'Or call your local emergency number' is our own line and gets no tag.
Do not use the standard don't-stop line here, because the label advises stopping and seeking medical attention if a hypersensitivity reaction occurs. Use instead: 'If it is only a mild rash or itch, call your prescriber before your next dose, and let them decide whether you keep going.' Make it one clause per card and do not run it through the auto-splitter.
Then 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line back to sentence 1. No digits or contractions in the narration outside the fixed lines, and no 'now' or 'new'.
The title can stay as 'Tirzepatide Itchy Rash: Allergy or Normal? #shorts', or use the safer 'Tirzepatide and Itchy Rash: What the Label Says #shorts'.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide Itchy Rash: Allergy or Normal? #shorts
pieces.why:
Replaces the held 08:00 hair Short with another proven 'Is this normal?' visible body moment. Every fact comes from one label section and its Medication Guide, so it should pass the fact-check first time. No other piece today covers skin or allergy. | fact-check: The topic is fine: it's a real, evergreen question, it's on-label, and it helps keep viewers safe. But I checked the current Zepbound label on DailyMed (Revised 11/2026, DailyMed updated 16 Nov 2026, setid 487cd7e7-434c-4925-99fa-aa80b1cc776b), and three parts of the brief don't match it.
(1) The planned stat '5 in 100 vs 3 in 100' is not in section 6.1. The label splits reactions into two types and gives no combined figure: 'immediate hypersensitivity reactions (within one day after drug administration) occurred in 2.1% of ZEPBOUND-treated patients compared to 0.4% of placebo-treated patients, while non-immediate hypersensitivity reactions occurred in 3.5% … compared to 2.7%'. Adding the two together ourselves would be our own arithmetic presented as the label's number.
(2) The label never says 'most weren't serious'. Its words are: 'The majority of the hypersensitivity reactions in trials were skin reactions (e.g., rash, itching).' Section 5.6 adds that severe reactions occurred in 0.1% on Zepbound vs no one on placebo, and that serious reactions (anaphylaxis, angioedema) were seen in postmarketing reports.
(3) This is a safety conflict. Section 5.6 says: 'If hypersensitivity reactions occur, advise patients to promptly seek medical attention and discontinue use of ZEPBOUND.' Following a rash Short with the standard 'don't stop or change your medicine on your own' line could be read as 'keep injecting through an allergic reaction', which goes against the label. The mild 'worth telling your prescriber' line also understates the label's 'promptly'.
Two smaller points. The pool is Studies 1 and 2, so the card should name both: Study 1 had no type 2 diabetes, Study 2 had type 2 diabetes only. I could not read the Medication Guide text through the tool, so the allergy list in the brief is not confirmed and must be checked against the Medication Guide PDF (Revised 11/2026). 'Or call your local emergency number' is our own line and gets no source tag. The working title is acceptable, but 'Normal?' should not suggest that a rash is expected.
